Habit and relationship
Tree, shrub and herb describe growth forms, not families. A family may contain several growth forms; a species can change its appearance with age and habitat.
Leaf or leaflet?
A simple leaf has one blade, even when lobed. A compound leaf has several leaflets. A bud at the base of the leaf stalk helps identify the whole leaf; there is no bud at the base of each leaflet.
Alternate, opposite, whorled
Inspect a twig: one leaf per node is alternate; two are opposite; three or more form a whorl. A rosette gathers leaves on a very short stem.
Margin and veins
Margins can be entire, toothed or lobed. Veins may branch along a central axis or radiate from the base. Examine the whole leaf and both surfaces.
One flower or a hundred?
In Asteraceae, a head contains many small florets on one receptacle. In oxeye daisy, the white rays belong to flowers distinct from those of the yellow disc.
Umbels and clusters
In an umbel, several flower stalks arise from roughly the same point. A compound umbel bears smaller umbels. A flat flower cluster is not automatically an umbel.
The pea flower
A pea flower has a large upper standard petal, two lateral wings and a keel formed by the two lower petals. This structure occurs in the Fabaceae shown here.
Fruit and seed
In flowering plants, fruit develops from the ovary, sometimes with other tissues. It contains seeds. Pods, samaras and acorns are fruits; a conker is a seed inside a capsule.
Conifers
Conifers produce pollen cones and cones bearing ovules and then seeds. They lack flowers and fruits in the angiosperm sense. Larch sheds its needles every autumn.
Observing grasses
Poaceae bear reduced flowers in spikelets. Spikelet arrangement, glumes, awns and the junction of sheath and blade are useful features. Their flowers are often inconspicuous but present.
Observing through the seasons
Plants change: buds, leaves, flowers and fruits provide complementary features. Timing varies with region, elevation and weather. A calendar is a guide, not a guaranteed date.
Scientific names and synonyms
A species name combines a genus and an epithet. Common names vary by region. Research can move a species to another genus or family; older names then provide useful search synonyms.
Pedunculate oak
Quercus robur
Chêne pédonculé
Very short leaf stalk with small basal lobes. Acorns on long stalks. The two oaks can hybridise: examine several features.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sessile oak
Quercus petraea
Chêne sessile
Well-developed leaf stalk; leaf base usually wedge-shaped without pronounced basal lobes. Acorns nearly stalkless on the twig. Intermediate forms occur.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European beech
Fagus sylvatica
Hêtre commun
Smooth grey bark. Young leaf margins are hairy, scarcely toothed or untoothed; buds are long and pointed. Triangular beechnuts in a bristly cup.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European hornbeam
Carpinus betulus
Charme commun

Doubly toothed leaves with prominent lateral veins. Buds lie against the twig. The small dry fruit is a ribbed nutlet carried by a large three-lobed bract. The winglike organ is this supporting bract, separate from the fruit wall.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Silver birch
Betula pendula
Bouleau verruqueux
White bark, dark and fissured at the base of older trunks. Slender, often drooping twigs bear small warts. Triangular leaves and tiny winged fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common alder
Alnus glutinosa
Aulne glutineux
Rounded leaves, often notched at the tip. Long hanging male catkins; woody female fruiting structures resemble small cones, but this is not a conifer.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Field maple
Acer campestre
Érable champêtre
Small leaves with five rather rounded lobes. Twigs sometimes bear corky ridges. The two samara wings spread widely, nearly in a straight line.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Norway maple
Acer platanoides
Érable plane
Leaf lobes end in long points. Upright flower clusters, often before the leaves. Samara wings form a very wide angle.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sycamore maple
Acer pseudoplatanus
Érable sycomore
Large five-lobed toothed leaves. Flowers in hanging racemes. Samara wings are closer together than in Norway maple; older bark flakes in plates.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common ash
Fraxinus excelsior
Frêne commun
Black buds and opposite leaves, usually with 7–13 toothed leaflets. Flowers lack petals and appear before the leaves. Elongated winged dry fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Small-leaved lime
Tilia cordata
Tilleul à petites feuilles
Heart-shaped leaves with an asymmetric base; small rusty hair tufts below vein junctions. Flowers and fruits are attached to a long pale bract.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sweet chestnut
Castanea sativa
Châtaignier commun
Long simple leaves with sharp teeth. Long upright catkins. Burr densely covered in slender spines, usually enclosing several chestnuts.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Horse chestnut
Aesculus hippocastanum
Marronnier d’Inde
Opposite leaves with 5–7 large leaflets meeting at one point. Upright flower panicles. Sparsely spiny capsules contain one or a few large seeds.
Native to the Balkans; widely planted in French parks and avenues.
Wild cherry
Prunus avium
Merisier
Toothed leaves, often with two red glands on the stalk. Bark with horizontal lenticels. White flowers in small clusters; long-stalked cherries.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Rowan
Sorbus aucuparia
Sorbier des oiseleurs
Alternate leaves, usually with 9–15 toothed leaflets. White flowers in dense clusters. Small orange-red pomes, not true botanical berries.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European aspen
Populus tremula
Peuplier tremble
Rounded mature leaves with long flattened stalks that flutter in the wind. Young shoot leaves may be more triangular. Catkins precede the leaves; seeds have cottony hairs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Scots pine
Pinus sylvestris
Pin sylvestre
Needles in pairs, slightly twisted. Upper trunk often orange. Egg-shaped cones with woody scales mature over more than one season.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Silver fir
Abies alba
Sapin pectiné
Flat, usually blunt needles with two pale bands underneath. Upright cones break apart on the tree, leaving their central axis behind.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Norway spruce
Picea abies
Épicéa commun
Sharp four-sided needles attached all around the twig on small pegs. Long hanging cones fall intact.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European larch
Larix decidua
Mélèze d’Europe
Soft needles in tufts on short shoots, single on long shoots. Needles turn yellow and fall in autumn. Small upright cones remain on the branches.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common hazel
Corylus avellana
Noisetier commun
Often has several stems from the base. Broad hairy leaves with a heart-shaped base. Male catkins in winter; tiny female flowers with red stigmas. Nuts in leafy husks.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common hawthorn
Crataegus monogyna
Aubépine monogyne
Thorny twigs. Deeply lobed leaves; small five-petalled flowers usually have one style. Red fruits usually contain one stone; hybridisation with other hawthorns occurs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Blackthorn
Prunus spinosa
Prunellier
Shrub with many thorny twigs. Small toothed leaves. White flowers often precede the leaves; blue-black sloes have a pale waxy bloom.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Dog rose
Rosa canina
Églantier
Arching stems with hooked prickles. Leaves usually have 5–7 leaflets. Five-petalled flowers; red hips contain the small dry fruits. The dog-rose group is complex.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common elder
Sambucus nigra
Sureau noir
Opposite leaves with 5–7 toothed leaflets. Broad flat clusters of tiny cream flowers. Black fruits in drooping clusters when ripe; twigs have white pith.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Guelder rose
Viburnum opulus
Viorne obier
Opposite three-lobed leaves. Large sterile flowers surround small fertile central flowers. Translucent red fruits; the wild form differs from snowball cultivars.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common dogwood
Cornus sanguinea
Cornouiller sanguin
Opposite leaves with lateral veins curving towards the tip. Young twigs often red. White four-petalled flowers and black fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European spindle
Euonymus europaeus
Fusain d’Europe
Opposite finely toothed leaves; green, sometimes angular twigs. Small four-petalled flowers. Pink four-lobed capsules reveal bright orange seed coverings.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common holly
Ilex aquifolium
Houx commun
Thick glossy leaves, often spiny low down but sometimes entire higher up. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. Red fruits on female plants.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common box
Buxus sempervirens
Buis commun
Small opposite leathery leaves with rounded or slightly notched tips. Yellowish flowers without petals in leaf axils. Capsules end in three small points.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Wild privet
Ligustrum vulgare
Troène commun
Opposite entire leaves, sometimes retained through part of winter. Tiny white four-lobed flowers in terminal panicles. Black fruits; leaf retention depends on climate.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common broom
Cytisus scoparius
Genêt à balais
Green angled stems without spines. Lower leaves often have three leaflets, upper leaves are simple; some fall early. Large yellow flowers and dark pods with hairy margins.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common gorse
Ulex europaeus
Ajonc d’Europe
Dense shrub with many spiny shoots and spine-like leaves. Yellow flowers with a hairy calyx; short hairy pods. Flowering may extend well beyond the main season.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common heather
Calluna vulgaris
Callune commune
Tiny opposite scale-like leaves in four rows. Small pink flowers with four coloured sepals longer than the corolla. A dwarf shrub of acid soils.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Bell heather
Erica cinerea
Bruyère cendrée
Small narrow leaves in whorls of three. Purple-pink urn-shaped corolla with four small lobes. Unlike the scale-leaved common heather.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common daisy
Bellis perennis
Pâquerette vivace
All leaves form a spoon-leaved basal rosette. Each leafless stalk carries one head: white, sometimes pink, ray florets surround yellow tubular florets.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Oxeye daisy
Leucanthemum vulgare
Marguerite commune
Stems bear alternate leaves; basal leaves are broader than upper leaves. Large white-and-yellow flower heads. Several related oxeye daisies require detailed examination.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common yarrow
Achillea millefolium
Achillée millefeuille
Finely divided feathery leaves. Many tiny white or pinkish heads form a flat cluster; each head has a few short ray florets.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Brown knapweed
Centaurea jacea
Centaurée jacée
Purple heads of tubular florets, often enlarged around the edge. Involucral bracts have brown fringed appendages. Variable and similar to other knapweeds.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common poppy
Papaver rhoeas
Coquelicot
Stem with spreading hairs and a nodding flower bud. Four crumpled red petals, sometimes black at the base. Rounded capsule topped by a radiating disc and opening through pores.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Meadow buttercup
Ranunculus acris
Renoncule âcre
Leaves deeply divided into narrow segments. Upright flowers have five glossy yellow petals and many stamens. Small achenes form a head; several buttercups look alike.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Lesser celandine
Ficaria verna
Ranunculus ficaria; ficaire
Shiny heart-shaped leaves, sometimes dark-marked. Spring flowers usually have 8–12 narrow petals and three sepals. Foliage usually disappears after spring.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cowslip
Primula veris
Primevère officinale
Rosette of wrinkled leaves. A stalk bears several flowers nodding to one side; yellow corollas with small orange marks and inflated pale calyces.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common foxglove
Digitalis purpurea
Digitale pourpre
A large rosette precedes the leafy stem. Long raceme of hanging tubular flowers, often facing one side; spotted inside. Capsules hold numerous tiny seeds.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Harebell
Campanula rotundifolia
Campanule à feuilles rondes
Rounded basal leaves often disappear by flowering; stem leaves are narrow and elongated. Blue five-lobed bell flowers. Look for both leaf types.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sweet violet
Viola odorata
Violette odorante
Heart-shaped leaves; flowers have five unequal petals and a rear spur. A creeping, stolon-forming plant, usually with scented flowers. Other violets require examination of stipules and hairs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Red clover
Trifolium pratense
Trèfle des prés
Three oval leaflets, often with a pale chevron. Upright hairy stems. Pink to purple pea flowers form dense heads close to the upper leaves.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
White clover
Trifolium repens
Trèfle blanc
Creeping stems root at the nodes. Three rounded leaflets, often pale-marked. White flower heads on long stalks; older flowers bend downwards.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common bird’s-foot trefoil
Lotus corniculatus
Lotier corniculé
Five leaflets: three at the tip and two near the base. Small clusters of yellow, sometimes orange-tinted flowers. Slender pods spread like toes.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Tufted vetch
Vicia cracca
Vesce cracca
Leaves have many narrow leaflets and end in a branched tendril. Climbs through surrounding vegetation. Long one-sided racemes of violet flowers; flattened pods.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Wild carrot
Daucus carota
Carotte sauvage
Stem and leaves usually hairy; leaves finely divided. Umbels have divided bracts, sometimes a dark central flower. Rays often curl into a nest at maturity.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cow parsley
Anthriscus sylvestris
Cerfeuil sauvage
Large finely divided triangular leaves. Spring white umbels usually lack large bracts beneath the main umbel. Long smooth dark fruits; many similar species occur in this family.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Ribwort plantain
Plantago lanceolata
Plantain lancéolé
Rosette of narrow leaves with 3–5 prominent lengthwise veins. Grooved leafless stalk ends in a short spike ringed by pale stamens during flowering.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Greater plantain
Plantago major
Grand plantain
Rosette of broad oval leaves with long stalks and strong curved veins. Long slender spikes of inconspicuous flowers. Common on compacted ground and paths.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Stinging nettle
Urtica dioica
Grande ortie
Opposite coarsely toothed leaves; stems and leaves bear stinging hairs. Tiny greenish flowers in axillary clusters; male and female flowers usually on separate plants.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
White dead-nettle
Lamium album
Lamier blanc
Opposite toothed nettle-like leaves without stinging hairs. Square stem. Large white two-lipped flowers cluster around the stem at the nodes.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Meadow sage
Salvia pratensis
Sauge des prés
Large wrinkled basal leaves and opposite stem leaves. Blue-violet flowers have an arched upper lip and form spaced tiers; two fertile stamens.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cock’s-foot
Dactylis glomerata
Dactyle aggloméré
Tufted grass; young leaves are folded and sheaths flattened. Panicle has dense spikelet clusters, often facing one side. A membranous ligule is visible.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Perennial ryegrass
Lolium perenne
Ivraie vivace
Leaves often glossy underneath. Simple spike: alternate spikelets are set edge-on to the axis. Usually awnless; small auricles clasp the stem.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Quaking grass
Briza media
Brize intermédiaire
Airy panicle with small hanging heart-shaped spikelets on fine stalks. Spikelets are often purple-tinged and tremble in the wind. Narrow leaves.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
The two oaks
Compare leaf stalks and acorn stalks: short leaf stalks and long acorn stalks in pedunculate oak; longer leaf stalks and nearly stalkless acorns in sessile oak. Hybrids can blur these differences.
Beech and hornbeam
Beech has scarcely toothed leaf margins, hairy when young; hornbeam has strong teeth and prominent veins. Also compare buds and fruits.
Three maples
Field maple: small rounded lobes and nearly aligned samaras. Norway maple: long points and widely spreading wings. Sycamore: toothed lobes and hanging flower racemes.
Four conifers
Pine: needles in pairs. Larch: tufts of deciduous needles. Fir: flat needles and upright cones. Spruce: four-sided needles and hanging cones. Inspect twigs rather than habit alone.
Sweet and horse chestnut
Sweet chestnut: simple toothed leaf, burr with numerous fine spines. Horse chestnut: palmately compound leaf, capsule with widely spaced spines; the conker is a seed.
Compound leaves
Ash and elder: opposite leaves; rowan: alternate leaves. Ash has winged fruits, rowan orange-red fruits and elder black fruits.
Thorny hedgerow shrubs
Hawthorn: lobed leaves. Blackthorn: small simple toothed leaves. Dog rose: compound leaves and hooked prickles. White or pink flowers alone do not distinguish them.
Heather and bell heather
Common heather: tiny opposite scale leaves and visible coloured sepals. Bell heather: narrow leaves in threes and an urn-shaped corolla.
Broom and gorse
Common broom has green angled shoots without spines; gorse forms a dense network of spines. Both bear yellow pea flowers and pods.
Daisy and oxeye daisy
Daisy: small rosette and leafless stalk. Oxeye daisy: taller leafy stem and usually larger flower head. Yellow discs and white rays consist of many florets.
Buttercup and celandine
Meadow buttercup: divided leaves, usually five petals. Lesser celandine: heart-shaped leaves, usually eight to twelve petals, mainly spring flowering.
Two clovers
Red clover: upright hairy stems and pink heads. White clover: creeping stems rooting at nodes and long-stalked white heads. Pale leaflet markings vary.
Two umbellifers
Wild carrot: divided bracts below the umbel and bristly fruits. Cow parsley: no large bracts below the main umbel and long smooth fruits. This comparison does not cover the many other Apiaceae.
Two plantains
Ribwort plantain: narrow leaves and short spike. Greater plantain: broad stalked leaves and long slender spike. Both have strong lengthwise or curved veins.
Nettle and dead-nettle
Stinging nettle: stinging hairs and tiny greenish flowers. White dead-nettle: no stinging hairs and white two-lipped flowers. Do not use skin contact as a test.
Three grasses
Cock’s-foot: dense spikelet clusters. Perennial ryegrass: spikelets attached alternately along one axis. Quaking grass: heart-shaped spikelets hanging on fine stalks.
Quercus ilex
Holm oak
Yeuse; chêne yeuse; evergreen oak
Evergreen, leathery leaves are dark above and pale felted beneath. Margins range from nearly entire to spiny, especially on young shoots. Acorns sit in cups with small, appressed scales.
Dry Mediterranean woods and scrub; also occurs along the Atlantic coast and is planted elsewhere.
Quercus pubescens
Downy oak
Chêne blanc; white oak

A spreading oak with an irregular crown. Young twigs and leaf undersides are hairy; leaves have rounded lobes and a distinct stalk. Acorns are nearly sessile or shortly stalked. Dead leaves may persist in winter.
Warm slopes, often on limestone; frequent in southern France and locally farther north.
Acer monspessulanum
Montpellier maple
Érable trilobé; Montpellier maple
Small, opposite, thick leaves have three usually untoothed lobes. The paired fruit wings are held close together, almost parallel. Often a small, low-branching tree.
Open woods and dry slopes in southern France, with scattered populations farther north.
Tilia platyphyllos
Large-leaved lime
Tilleul à larges feuilles; large leaved linden
Large heart-shaped leaves are hairy beneath, with pale hair tufts at vein junctions. Hanging flowers share an elongated bract. The small, hard fruits have five prominent ribs.
Ravine woods, cool slopes and mountains; also planted in parks and villages.
Betula pubescens
Downy birch
Bouleau blanc pubescent; downy birch

Young shoots are hairy and usually lack the resinous warts of silver birch. Ovate leaves have rounded bases and irregular teeth. Branches tend to be less drooping; female catkins release tiny winged fruits.
Damp acidic soils, bogs, cool woods and mountains; scarce in Mediterranean regions.
Populus nigra
Black poplar
Liard; peuplier d’Italie; Lombardy poplar

Finely toothed, triangular to diamond-shaped leaves and deeply fissured bark. Reddish male and female catkins occur on separate trees. Capsules release cottony seeds. The plate shows the spreading habit, rather than the Lombardy cultivar.
Riverbanks and floodplain woods; planted hybrid poplars can be difficult to distinguish.
Salix alba
White willow
Saule argenté; silver willow
Long, finely toothed lanceolate leaves have silky hairs, especially beneath. Catkins appear with the leaves. Male and female trees are separate; capsules release seeds with long hairs.
Riverbanks, ditches and floodplains across much of France.
Prunus padus
Bird cherry
Bois puant; putier; bird cherry
Long racemes of white flowers develop into small black drupes. Alternate, toothed leaves often have two glands near the top of the stalk. The bark bears conspicuous lenticels.
Cool woods, streamsides and valleys, especially in northern and eastern France and the mountains.
Malus sylvestris
Crab apple
Pommier des bois; wild apple

A small tree with sometimes spine-tipped short shoots. Mature leaves are almost hairless beneath; pink buds open into whitish flowers. Small apples retain their calyx. Hybrids with cultivated apples complicate identification.
Woodland edges and hedges, usually scattered across much of France.
Ulmus minor
Field elm
Ormeau; smooth-leaved elm

Short-stalked leaves have strongly unequal bases and double teeth. Small flowers without petals appear before the leaves. Rounded samaras are notched at the tip, with the seed near the notch; suckering is frequent.
Hedges, woods and valleys; often survives as young suckers where Dutch elm disease has removed mature trees.
Viburnum lantana
Wayfaring tree
Mancienne; viorne mancienne; wayfaring tree
Opposite, thick, wrinkled oval leaves are felted beneath. All the small flowers in the cluster are fertile. Drupes turn from green to red and then black, often at different stages within one cluster.
Rather dry hedges and woodland edges, especially on limestone.
Cornus mas
Cornelian cherry
Cornelier; cornier; cornelian cherry
Small yellow umbels appear before the leaves. Opposite, entire leaves have curved lateral veins. Elongated red drupes contain a hard stone. Unlike common dogwood, its flowers are yellow.
Open woods, hedges and limestone slopes; also cultivated.
Crataegus laevigata
Midland hawthorn
Épine blanche; aubépine épineuse; Crataegus oxyacantha
Leaves are shallowly lobed, mainly in their upper half. Flowers usually have two styles, sometimes three; fruits normally contain two stones. Hybridisation with common hawthorn is frequent.
Hedges and woods, especially in cooler temperate parts of France.
Frangula alnus
Alder buckthorn
Rhamnus frangula; aulne noir; alder buckthorn
A thornless shrub with alternate, entire leaves and curved lateral veins. Tiny greenish five-parted flowers sit in leaf axils. Drupes turn red and then black; twigs have pale lenticels.
Damp woods and heaths, often on acidic soils; widespread outside the driest districts.
Rhamnus cathartica
Purging buckthorn
Nerprun cathartique; common buckthorn
Shoots often end in a spine. Opposite to subopposite, sometimes alternate leaves are finely toothed, with a few strong curved veins. Greenish flowers have four parts; ripe drupes are black.
Hedges, scrub and open woodland, often on limestone.
Salix caprea
Goat willow
Marsault; saule des chèvres; pussy willow
A large shrub or small tree with broad, wrinkled leaves, felted beneath. Oval male catkins turn from silver to yellow before the leaves emerge. Female plants later bear capsules with silky seeds.
Woodland edges, clearings and fresh soils; tolerates drier ground than many willows.
Genista tinctoria
Dyer’s greenweed
Herbe à jaunir; dyers greenweed
A thornless small shrub with simple lanceolate leaves. Yellow pea flowers cluster at shoot tips, followed by elongated pods. Unlike broom, its leaves remain simple.
Heaths, nutrient-poor grassland and sunny woodland edges across much of France.
Amelanchier ovalis
Snowy mespilus
Amelanchier rotundifolia; amélanchier commun; snowy mespilus
Toothed oval leaves are white-felted beneath when young. Short racemes bear flowers with five narrow, elongated white petals. Small bluish-black pome fruits retain their calyx.
Limestone rocks, scrub and open woods, especially in southern France and mountain districts.
Vaccinium myrtillus
Bilberry
Brimbelle; airelle myrtille; European blueberry

A small deciduous shrub with angular green stems. Leaves are finely toothed; solitary urn-shaped flowers are pinkish to greenish. Bloom-coated blue-black berries have coloured flesh, unlike many large cultivated blueberries.
Acidic woodland, heaths and mountains; scarce on lowland limestone.
Prunus mahaleb
St Lucie cherry
Bois de Sainte-Lucie; mahaleb cherry
A shrub or small tree with rounded, shiny, finely crenate leaves. Small clusters of fragrant white flowers produce pea-sized black drupes. Leaves are rounder than those of wild cherry.
Dry slopes, hedges and open woodland, mainly on limestone; frequent in southern and eastern France.
Cichorium intybus
Chicory
Barbe de capucin; chicory

Stiff branching stems rise above divided basal leaves; upper leaves are smaller. Blue heads consist entirely of five-toothed strap-shaped florets. Short fruits carry minute scales, without a large feathery parachute.
Road verges, tracksides and dry grasslands; widespread.
Matricaria chamomilla
German chamomile
Camomille allemande; Matricaria recutita; Chamomilla recutita; scented mayweed

An aromatic annual with leaves twice divided into very fine segments. Heads have white rays and a yellow disc; the receptacle becomes conical and is hollow, as shown in section. Fruits are small and ribbed.
Fields, waste ground and paths; frequency varies between regions.
Cardamine pratensis
Cuckooflower
Cressonnette; cresson des prés; lady’s smock

Basal leaves have fairly rounded leaflets, while stem leaflets are narrow. Pale flowers have four petals and six stamens, two shorter than the others. Long siliques open by two valves to release the seeds.
Damp meadows, ditches and stream margins, from lowlands to mountains.
Capsella bursa-pastoris
Shepherd’s purse
Bourse à pasteur; shepherds purse
Rosette leaves vary from entire to deeply divided; stem leaves clasp the stem. Tiny white flowers have four petals. The lengthening raceme bears triangular, inverted heart-shaped silicles.
Gardens, fields, pavements and disturbed ground throughout France; may flower nearly year-round in mild weather.
Silene dioica
Red campion
Silène dioïque; Lychnis dioica; red campion

A hairy plant with opposite leaves. Five deeply notched pink petals emerge from a fused calyx; male and female flowers are on separate plants. The plate shows a female flower with five styles. Capsules open by ten rolled-back teeth.
Cool woodland edges, hedges and damp woods; scarcer in the dry south.
Rabelera holostea
Greater stitchwort
Stellaria holostea; langue d’oiseau; greater stitchwort

Narrow, opposite, stalkless leaves have rough margins. Each flower has five white petals split about halfway, rather than ten petals. Capsules have six teeth. Many floras still use the name Stellaria holostea.
Hedges, shady banks and woodland edges, often forming springtime patches.
Geranium robertianum
Herb-robert
Herbe à Robert; bec de grue; herb Robert
Often reddish, hairy stems carry leaves deeply divided into three to five further-cut segments. Five-petalled pink flowers usually occur in pairs. The fruit has a long beak above five mericarps.
Woods, old walls, banks and shady gardens; very widespread.
Malva sylvestris
Common mallow
Grande mauve; mauve des bois; tall mallow

Rounded leaves have five to seven lobes and crenate margins. Five notched mauve petals bear darker veins; stamens are united into a column. The flat, wheel-shaped fruit is made of mericarps arranged around the centre.
Waste ground, roadsides and hedges, especially on enriched soils; widespread.
Veronica chamaedrys
Germander speedwell
Fausse germandrée; germander speedwell

Opposite toothed leaves and two lines of hairs on the stem. Lateral racemes bear blue flowers with white throats. The corolla has four unequal lobes and two stamens; capsules are flattened and heart-shaped.
Meadows, hedges, banks and open woods; common across much of France.
Potentilla reptans
Creeping cinquefoil
Quintefeuille; five-finger grass; creeping cinquefoil
Long runners root at their nodes. Long-stalked palmate leaves usually have five toothed leaflets. Solitary yellow flowers have five petals; many small achenes collect on the receptacle.
Grasslands, paths, ditches and compacted ground, often damp; very widespread.

Woody plants with alternate, often unequal-based toothed leaves. Elms have small flowers without petals and flat winged fruits.

Oaks of dry woodland

Holm oak: evergreen, thick, unlobed leaves, often spiny. Downy oak: lobed leaves and hairy young shoots and undersides. Sessile oak: lobed deciduous leaves, generally less hairy; stalks and leaf bases also matter.
Two birches

Silver birch: warty young shoots, more triangular leaves and often drooping branchlets. Downy birch: hairy young shoots, rounder leaf bases and usually more upright branchlets. Hybrids and variable leaves can blur these distinctions.
Two limes

Small-leaved lime: mostly hairless leaves with rusty hair tufts beneath and weakly ribbed fruits. Large-leaved lime: generally larger, hairier leaves with pale tufts, and hard fruits with prominent ribs. Leaf size alone is unreliable.
White willow and goat willow

White willow: long, narrow, silky leaves; slender catkins appear with the leaves. Goat willow: broad wrinkled leaves, felted beneath; oval male catkins appear before the leaves. Female catkins differ from the male plates.
Two hawthorns

Common hawthorn usually has deeply cut leaves, one style and one stone per fruit. Midland hawthorn usually has shallower lobes, two styles and two stones. Hybrids are frequent; inspect several flowers or fruits.
Alder and purging buckthorn

Alder buckthorn: thornless, alternate entire leaves, five-parted flowers. Purging buckthorn: often spine-tipped shoots, opposite or subopposite toothed leaves, four-parted flowers. Both develop black fleshy fruits.
Two viburnums
Guelder rose has lobed leaves, conspicuous sterile marginal flowers and red fruits. Wayfaring tree has unlobed felted leaves, uniformly small fertile flowers and fruits turning black.
Silique and silicle

Cuckooflower has pale pink to white flowers and long narrow siliques. Shepherd’s purse has tiny white flowers and short triangular silicles. Both fruits open by two valves around a seed-bearing partition; neither is a legume.
Three types of flower head

Oxeye daisy: white rays around a yellow disc, simple leaves. German chamomile: white rays and yellow disc, finely divided leaves, hollow conical receptacle. Chicory: blue head made entirely of ligulate florets, no yellow disc.

African baobab
Adansonia digitata

Massive trunk and stout branches. Adult leaves have usually five to seven leaflets; young plants may bear simple leaves. Large hanging flowers have five white petals and a dense brush of stamens. The velvety woody fruit stays closed around dry pulp and seeds.
Widespread in seasonally dry tropical Africa, particularly savannas; also planted near settlements.
Umbrella thorn
Acacia tortilis · acacia raddiana

A spreading crown often forms an umbrella. Tiny leaflets are carried on paired pinnae. Long straight thorns and short hooked thorns may coexist. Cream flower heads give way to narrow, coiled, usually indehiscent pods.
Dry African savannas and semi-desert regions, from northern and Sahelian areas to eastern and southern Africa; forms vary by subspecies.
Apple-ring acacia
Acacia albida · kad · cad · gao

Large tree with pale young twigs and paired straight stipular thorns. Bipinnate leaves and slender creamy flower spikes. Thick orange-brown pods curl into open rings. Its often reversed leaf cycle is particularly distinctive.
Widespread through African savannas, alluvial plains and seasonal watercourses; frequently retained in cultivated fields.
Tamarind
Tamarin · tamarind

Dense rounded crown and leaves with many paired oblong leaflets, without a terminal leaflet or tendril. Three conspicuous yellow petals carry red veins; two other petals are reduced. Brown brittle pods remain closed around pulp and hard seeds.
Native to tropical Africa and widely cultivated throughout the tropics. African savannas, wooded sites and villages.
Desert date
Balanitès · desert date

Thorny tree with an open crown. Each leaf bears exactly two leathery leaflets. Small greenish-yellow flowers have five petals and ten stamens. The elongated drupe contains one hard stone; despite its name, this is not a palm.
Very widespread in dry tropical Africa, notably the Sahel and eastern Africa; also occurs beyond Africa.
Sodom apple
Calotrope · arbre à soie · Sodom apple
Upright shrub with thick, nearly stalkless opposite leaves and milky latex. The waxy five-lobed corolla surrounds a five-parted corona. Inflated follicles release flat seeds with silky tufts.
Dry northern and tropical Africa, especially sandy disturbed ground, roadsides and overgrazed areas; also native in southwestern Asia.
Senegal senna
Cassia italica · Cassia obovata · séné d’Italie

Low perennial or subshrub with paired, blunt leaflets and no terminal tendril. Yellow flowers have five unequal petals and conspicuous unequal anthers. The flattened pods are curved. Habit and hairiness vary among subspecies.
Dry sandy or stony habitats across much of Africa, including the Sahel; its native range extends to the Indian subcontinent.
Guiera
Nguer · guier · n’guère

Much-branched shrub with small grey-green, softly hairy leaves, usually opposite. Cream flower heads have projecting stamens. Long spindle-shaped silky fruits radiate from the same head, producing a distinctive spider-like cluster.
Savannas from Senegal to Sudan. Often abundant on sandy soils and degraded fallows in the Sahelian and Sudanian zones.
Kinkeliba
Kinkeliba · quinquéliba · Combretum raimbaultii
Spreading shrub, sometimes a small tree or scrambling climber. Opposite leaves become reddish-brown when old. Small white flowers occur in short spikes; the dry reddish fruit has four papery wings.
West Africa to the Central African Republic, in savanna scrub, rocky sites and woodland margins. The illustrated habit is shrubby.
Indian jujube
Jujube · ber · Ziziphus mauritiana

Thorny shrub or tree with drooping branches. The shiny leaves show three strong veins from the base and a pale hairy underside. Tiny greenish flowers grow in axillary clusters. Wild drupes are smaller than those of many cultivated forms.
Widespread in warm African drylands and cultivated near settlements; also widespread in Asia. It may grow as a tree where conditions permit.
Buffel grass
Pennisetum ciliare · buffel grass

Tufted perennial grass with narrow blades. Its dense false spike is purple when young, becoming straw-coloured. Bristles surround groups of spikelets and remain with the dispersal unit. The true fruit is a small caryopsis.
Common in warm dry parts of Africa, especially open sandy habitats; also planted as pasture and present outside Africa.
Common thatching grass
Hyparrhénie hérissée · chaume · thatching grass

Dense perennial tussock with wiry culms. The inflorescence branches into pairs of hairy racemes, each pair accompanied by a spatheole. Long bent awns extend from fertile spikelets; they are not petals.
Widespread in African grasslands and open disturbed sites, particularly familiar in southern Africa; also native in the Mediterranean and southwestern Asia.
Winged-seed sesame
Sésame de gazelle · Sesamopteris alata

Annual with generally opposite leaves, rarely alternate, strongly differing along the stem: lower leaves are deeply divided or have three to five narrow leaflets; upper leaves are simple. Pink tubular flowers have darker lines on the lower lip. Beaked capsules contain seeds winged at both ends.
Widespread in tropical Africa south to Namibia and South Africa; sandy roadsides, grasslands and seasonal river beds.
Flower-of-an-hour
Hibiscus d’Afrique · ketmie d’Afrique · bladder hibiscus

Hairy annual with deeply divided leaves. Pale yellow petals have a dark purple base around the staminal column. A papery inflated, prominently veined calyx encloses the five-valved capsule. Flowers are short-lived.
Fields and disturbed open habitats. Native in the Mediterranean and parts of Eurasia; naturalized in much of eastern and southern Africa.
Creeping indigo

Prostrate to ascending perennial. Leaves usually bear seven leaflets inserted alternately along the rachis, broader near the tip. Dense racemes carry small pink to reddish pea flowers; short narrow pods turn downwards. Closely related Indigofera species require additional characters for identification.
Native across much of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Common in disturbed grassland, cultivated ground and fallows, often at moderate elevations.

Virginia rose

Suckering native rose with prickly stems and usually seven glossy, toothed leaflets. Open pink flowers have five petals and numerous stamens. Rounded red hips retain their sepals.

Perennial with rough, often three-veined leaves. Pink-purple ray florets spread or droop around a prominent spiny orange-brown cone of disc florets. The dry fruits are short angular cypselae, without a feathery pappus.

Wheat, rice and maize

Wheat bears a compact spike with several florets per spikelet. Rice bears a branched panicle with one fertile floret per spikelet and six stamens. Bulb, rhizome or pseudostem?

Bowiea stores reserves in a bulb of fleshy leaf bases; ginger has a branched underground stem, a rhizome. Clivia also has a rhizome, not an onion bulb. Banana leaf sheaths form the above-ground pseudostem. These organs are distinct even within monocots.
Three palms, different fruits

Coconut is a fibrous drupe with a hard inner wall; its white flesh is seed endosperm. The date has a thin membranous inner fruit wall: its hard central structure is the seed. The areca nut is also a seed, inside a fibrous drupe. Same family does not imply identical fruit anatomy.
One flower, many flowers, or a cone?

A pear pome contains accessory tissue around the ovary-derived core. Pineapple joins the products of many flowers into a syncarp. A fig encloses many tiny flowers and then fruits inside a fleshy receptacle. Juniper carries a fleshy seed cone, without an ovary: it is not a berry.

Palate, pouch and nectar spur

Snapdragon has a closed mouth and short basal pouch; toadflax has a long nectar spur. Bugle has a reduced upper lip and an open lower landing lip. Similar bilateral symmetry does not mean identical corolla anatomy.
Hairs, hooks and accessory envelopes

Pulsatilla carries persistent feathery styles on achenes. Coltsfoot has a pappus, a modified calyx on its one-seeded fruit. Agrimony hooks belong to the accessory hypanthium; bur medick hooks belong to the coiled pod. These appendages have different origins.

Upright, branching herb with open flat-topped flower umbels.

Anemarrhena; zhi mu
Rhizomatous perennial native to northern China and Mongolia. Long basal grasslike leaves contrast with a taller leafless flowering spike; the stout rhizome bears persistent fibrous leaf-base remains.

Clump of arching basal leaves with a separate upright flowering scape.

Canary Islands strawberry tree; Canary madrone

Evergreen tree endemic to the Canary Islands, with finely serrated leaves, peeling reddish bark, pendant bell-shaped flowers and orange granular fruits. It is related to the common strawberry tree but has distinctly orange ripe fruit.
Endemic to the Canary Islands.
Small evergreen tree with a spreading crown and peeling reddish bark.
Leathery lanceolate to elliptic leaves have fine saw-toothed margins.
Pale urn-shaped flowers hang in clusters from the branches.

Henequen; Yucatan sisal

A large, evergreen rosette-forming succulent with stiff, sword-shaped leaves edged by teeth and tipped with a spine. Mature plants send up a tall branched flowering stalk; the cultivated henequen is especially valued for strong leaf fibre. The plate shows a flowering plant and separate leaf and fibre details.
Native to Mexico and Central America; widely cultivated, especially in the Yucatan Peninsula.
Large perennial rosette; a mature individual produces a tall flowering panicle.
Stiff, long, lance-shaped leaves with marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine; leaves are harvested for fibre.

Shaw’s agave
Agave shawii
Shaw’s agave; coastal agave

A compact coastal agave forming a dense rosette of broad, fleshy leaves with conspicuous marginal teeth and a dark terminal spine. The adult flowering stalk rises far above the rosette and bears yellow flowers. Its restricted coastal habitat makes wild populations conservation-sensitive.
Coastal southern California and northwestern Baja California, including islands in the region.
A low, evergreen succulent rosette; flowering plants produce a much taller panicle.
Broad, thick leaves bear curved marginal teeth and a strong terminal spine.
Yellow flowers are carried on a tall, branched inflorescence.
A dry capsule follows flowering; plants commonly die after their single flowering event.
Lierre grimpant
Hedera helix
Lierre commun; English ivy

An evergreen woody climber that attaches to supports by aerial rootlets. Juvenile shoots carry alternate, palmately lobed leaves; flowering adult shoots instead bear unlobed leaves and rounded clusters of small greenish flowers. Blue-black berries mature later. Berries and other parts can cause illness if eaten, so the plant must not be confused with edible climbing plants.
Native from much of Europe and the Mediterranean region eastward to Iran; planted and naturalized elsewhere.
Evergreen climbing or ground-covering woody plant; adult flowering shoots are less clinging and have unlobed leaves.
Juvenile leaves are alternate and palmately lobed; adult flowering shoots have alternate, unlobed leaves.
Small greenish-yellow flowers form dense, rounded umbels in autumn.
Rounded berries ripen dark blue-black; they are not edible and can cause gastrointestinal upset.
Agrostide géante
Agrostis gigantea
Redtop; black bent

A tall perennial grass spreading by creeping rhizomes and forming leafy shoots. Its flat, narrow leaves sit below a large, open, finely branched panicle of tiny spikelets. The rhizomes and open inflorescence help distinguish it from compact, densely tufted bent grasses.
Native across temperate parts of Europe and Asia; introduced in many other regions.
Rhizomatous perennial grass, often forming loose colonies, with flowering stems that may exceed one metre.
Flat, narrow leaves arise from sheaths; a small ligule occurs where the blade meets its sheath.
A broad, open panicle bears many tiny, one-flowered spikelets.
Each spikelet forms a small grain-like caryopsis.
Baobab de Suarez
Adansonia suarezensis
Suarez baobab; northern baobab

A rare baobab endemic to northern Madagascar. Like other baobabs it is a large, seasonally deciduous tree with a massive trunk, palmately divided leaves and large flowers, followed by a woody-shelled fruit. The general baobab silhouette is well established, but exact proportions and some organ details vary among species; this plate is therefore schematic at species level.
Endemic to northern Madagascar, where it occurs in seasonally dry tropical vegetation.
Massive-trunked, seasonally deciduous tree; the flowering and leafless states occur at different times.
Leaves are palmately divided into several leaflets and are shed in the dry season.
Large pale flowers occur on long stalks; baobab flowers are short-lived.
An oblong fruit with a hard woody shell encloses dry pulp and numerous seeds.
Camomille des champs
Anthemis arvensis
Camomille sauvage; corn chamomile

An annual or short-lived herb with finely divided, aromatic leaves and daisy-like flower heads. Native across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia; introduced beyond this range.
Annual or short-lived herb, usually branched, with one or more flower heads on leafy stems.

White ray florets surround a yellow disc; the receptacle is conical and has pale scales between florets.

Buglosse des champs; petite buglosse

An annual, stiffly bristly herb with alternate, narrow leaves whose margins are wavy or shallowly toothed. Native to Europe; introduced in many temperate regions.
Usually branched annual herb, 15–60 cm tall, with coarse spreading bristles.
Alternate, narrow lance-shaped leaves are bristly and wavy-edged, with upper leaves clasping the stem.

Armoise maritime
Artemisia maritima
Armoise maritime; sea wormwood

A low aromatic perennial subshrub of northern and western European coasts. Its finely divided leaves are densely hairy and appear silvery; small yellow-brown flower heads are grouped along flowering branches. It is one of several aromatic wormwoods, so colour and scent alone are not a safe identification.
Native to northern and western Europe, including Atlantic and Baltic coastal regions.
Compact perennial subshrub, commonly 0.5–1 m high, with silvery branchlets.
Aromatic leaves are finely divided into very narrow, hair-covered segments that give a silvery appearance.
Tiny yellow-brown tubular florets form small nodding heads grouped on flowering stems.
Small dry achenes develop within the mature flower heads.
Asaret d’Europe
Asarum europaeum
Asaret d’Europe; European wild ginger

A low evergreen woodland perennial spreading by a creeping rhizome. Its glossy, long-stalked leaves are kidney-shaped to broadly heart-shaped. Solitary dark reddish-brown flowers lie close to the ground beneath the leaves; the three-lobed floral tube is unusual and easy to overlook. The common name “wild ginger” does not make it a culinary ginger.
Native from Europe eastward to central Siberia.
Low mat-forming perennial with a creeping rhizome and leaves borne in small pairs along its growth.
Glossy kidney-shaped or heart-shaped leaf on a long stalk, usually held close to the woodland floor.
A solitary, ground-level flower has a dark, three-lobed calyx forming a short jug-like tube.
A leathery capsule develops close to the ground after flowering.
Astrophytum tête-de-Méduse
Astrophytum caput-medusae
Tête-de-Méduse; Medusa-head cactus

A highly distinctive tuberous cactus native to northeastern Mexico. Instead of the usual ribbed cactus body, it bears a small basal caudex and long, narrow, tapering stem tubercles that radiate like serpents. Each tubercle carries an areole near its tip and is almost spineless. Large yellow flowers arise from mature tubercles; the long projections are modified stem, not leaves.
Endemic to northeastern Mexico, in Nuevo León and Tamaulipas.
Small tuberous cactus with a basal caudex and long radiating stem tubercles.
True leaves are absent; the long narrow projections are succulent stem tubercles with areoles near their tips.
A large yellow flower with a warm orange-red centre appears from a mature tubercle near the caudex.
A small scaly capsule forms after flowering and contains dark seeds.
Brocchinie carnivore
Brocchinia reducta
Brocchinie réduite; carnivorous bromeliad

A terrestrial bromeliad of the Guiana Shield highlands. Its narrow upright leaves overlap to form a persistent water-holding tank; waxy inner surfaces and modified absorptive scales help the plant trap insects and take up nutrients. This is a true documented case of carnivory within Bromeliaceae. The open branched flower stalk rises well above the rosette.
Native to the Guiana Shield, especially wet savannas, bogs and rocky tepui slopes in Venezuela and Guyana.
Terrestrial rosette-forming perennial, about 20–60 cm tall in flower, growing in open wet uplands.
Narrow upright leaves overlap at their bases to hold rainwater; the inner surface is waxy and bears absorptive scales.
A lax, branched panicle carries small pale yellow flowers above the rosette.
A dry capsule forms after flowering.
Cestre nocturne
Cestrum nocturnum
Cestre nocturne; jasmin de nuit

An evergreen tropical shrub, unrelated to true jasmines. Alternate glossy lance-shaped leaves accompany clusters of slender greenish-white tubular flowers that release a strong fragrance at night. Native from Mexico to Venezuela; widely cultivated and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions.
Evergreen, branching shrub, usually 1–3 m tall.
Simple, alternate, glossy lance-shaped leaves with entire margins.
Clusters of long greenish-white tubular flowers open mainly at night and are strongly scented.
Small pale berries follow flowering; they are poisonous and must not be eaten.

A large deciduous conifer from a restricted area of central China. Its fine feathery branchlets and leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, unlike the alternate sprays of coast redwood. Native to central China; widely planted elsewhere as an ornamental tree.
Tall, straight-trunked, conical tree with soft deciduous foliage and reddish-brown bark.

Common hop
Humulus lupulus
Common hop; hop

A rough, twining perennial vine arising from a persistent rhizome. Plants are usually male or female; female flowers form papery, cone-like clusters whose aromatic glands are used in brewing. The fruit is a small achene enclosed by the enlarged bracts.
Native from Europe across temperate Asia to Siberia and northern Iran, and in Morocco; cultivated and introduced widely.
Herbaceous perennial climber with annual twining stems that die back to the rhizome.

Passion fruit; purple granadilla; maracujá

A vigorous perennial liana with axillary tendrils and usually three-lobed leaves. Its solitary flowers have five sepals, five petals, a conspicuous many-ranked corona and a raised central reproductive column. The berry varies from yellow to purple according to cultivated form; do not use fruit colour alone to identify it.
Native to Brazil through Paraguay and northeastern Argentina; cultivated and naturalised throughout warm regions.
Climbing evergreen or seasonally deciduous vine supported by simple tendrils.
Alternate, usually three-lobed leaves have serrate edges; the leaf stalk commonly bears paired glands.

Lychee; litchi

Native from southern China through mainland Southeast Asia to Malaysia, Borneo and the Philippines; widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
Evergreen, round-crowned tree, usually branched from a short trunk.
Alternate paripinnate leaves bear opposite to subopposite entire leaflets, glossy above and paler beneath.

Jerusalem artichoke; sunroot; sunchoke

A tall perennial sunflower that spreads through underground rhizomes ending in edible tubers. Lower leaves are usually opposite and upper leaves alternate. Yellow heads contain an outer ring of ray florets and a central disc; the tubers are storage stems, not roots.
Native to central and eastern North America; cultivated and naturalised across temperate regions.
Coarse, upright perennial herb, often 1–3 m tall, arising from tuber-bearing rhizomes.
Broad, rough, toothed leaves are opposite below and alternate above, often with a rough underside.
Yellow composite heads have yellow ray florets around a darker disc of many small tubular florets.

Pink sundew; dwarf sundew

A tiny carnivorous wetland plant forming a flat rosette of sticky glandular leaves. Insects adhere to the tentacles and contribute nutrients in poor soils. Native from the southeastern United States through Mexico and the Caribbean to Central and South America.
Very low rosette, generally only a few centimetres across, with a slender upright flowering stalk.
Prostrate spatulate to nearly round blades are covered with red gland-tipped tentacles and sticky mucilage.

A small capsule contains minute ridged seeds after the petals fall.

A Sumatran highland pitcher plant that climbs or grows among mossy forest vegetation. Its leaves end in tendrils bearing distinctive upper pitchers: narrow below, funnel-shaped above, and with a nearly absent peristome. Endemic to montane western Sumatra, Indonesia.
Slender climbing or scrambling tropical perennial, often epiphytic in humid montane forest.
Alternate simple leaves have a prolonged midrib forming a tendril that terminates in a pitcher trap.

A rare shrub endemic to Mauritius. Like other hibiscus, it has alternate toothed leaves and large five-petaled flowers with a prominent staminal column; its species identity depends on the whole plant and provenance, not flower colour alone. Endemic to Mauritius, where remaining wild populations are very restricted; cultivated for conservation.
Woody, branching shrub of seasonally dry tropical slopes.

Succulent shrub with a large bottle-shaped caudex, branching above the base; height and shape vary among subspecies.
Simple narrow leaves form terminal rosettes on branches and may be shed in the dry season.

Paired narrow follicles split at maturity and release seeds, often with a tuft of hairs.

A tropical evergreen tree in the coffee family. Opposite broad leaves have curved secondary veins and small domatia in vein axils; rounded heads of many tiny flowers occur near branch tips. This description is botanical and does not imply that any plant part is safe to consume.
Native from mainland Southeast Asia through Malesia to New Guinea, often in wet lowland and riverine habitats.
Medium to large evergreen tree, sometimes with a buttressed base, growing in wet lowland forests.

Autumn narcissus; late narcissus

A small autumn-flowering bulbous geophyte of the western Mediterranean. One white flower bears six tepals and a very short yellow corona with a divided rim, among the smallest coronas in the genus. Native to the western Mediterranean, including the Iberian Peninsula and Morocco.
Small bulbous herb; flowers appear in autumn, with narrow leaves often developing later.

Powder-puff cactus; woolly nipple cactus

A small clustered cactus native to northeastern Mexico. Rounded stems bear tubercles with abundant fine white radial spines and a smaller number of stronger central spines, sometimes hooked. It has no true leaves: the conspicuous structures are spines arising from areoles.
Native to northeastern Mexico, extending south to Jalisco, in dry scrub and desert habitats.
Low, slowly clustering succulent with globose stems only a few centimetres across.
True leaves are absent; each tubercle bears an areole with fine hair-like radial spines and usually a few longer central spines.
Small pale cream to pink flowers form a ring near the stem apex.
Small red, elongated berries emerge among the tubercles after flowering.

Hippuris vulgaris
Common mare’s-tail; marestail

An aquatic perennial with erect emergent shoots and submerged forms in still or slow-moving freshwater. Numerous narrow leaves occur in close whorls along the stem. The tiny flowers are sessile in leaf axils and lack a perianth, unlike the conspicuous terminal cones of a horsetail (Equisetum).
Native across subarctic and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with scattered southern occurrences.
Rhizomatous aquatic herb rooted in mud; stems may rise above the water or remain submerged.
Narrow simple leaves occur in dense whorls; submerged leaves are softer and more elongated than emergent ones.
Minute sessile flowers sit in the upper leaf axils; they lack petals and sepals and have a single stamen.
A small one-seeded nut-like fruit develops in the leaf axil.

A rhizomatous African wetland sedge often grown as an ornamental. Its leafless triangular stems end in a radial umbrella-like whorl of long bracts around clusters of small spikelets. These apparent “leaves” are inflorescence bracts, not ordinary foliage.
Native to tropical and southern Africa, Madagascar and the Arabian Peninsula; naturalised or cultivated widely.
Tufted perennial sedge growing from a creeping rhizome, usually in shallow water or saturated soil.

Numerous small brownish spikelets cluster at the centre of the terminal bracts.
Each flower forms a tiny dry achene enclosed by the glumes of its spikelet.

Western bog laurel; little-leaf laurel

A low evergreen North American shrub of wet meadows, bog margins and alpine habitats. Opposite leathery leaves and terminal rose-purple flowers help distinguish it from related Kalmia. Like other laurels in the family, it is toxic if eaten.
Western North America from California and the Rocky Mountains north into Canada and Alaska.
Low spreading to upright shrub, about 5–80 cm high, often rooted in acidic wet ground.
Small opposite leathery leaves are elliptic to lance-shaped, with entire margins often slightly rolled under.
Rose-purple, saucer-shaped flowers occur singly or in terminal clusters; ten stamens are held in petal sacs before anthesis.
A small five-celled capsule releases tiny winged seeds.

Nothotsuga longibracteata
Bristlecone hemlock; long-bracted hemlock

A rare evergreen conifer endemic to southern China. Its needles spread radially rather than forming a flat two-ranked spray, and its nearly upright seed cones carry conspicuous bracts extending beyond the scales. Older floras may list it as Tsuga longibracteata; the accepted genus here follows POWO.
Endemic to montane southern China, mainly at low to middle elevations.
Narrow evergreen tree with horizontal branches and a dense conical crown.
Short linear needles are radially arranged around the shoots, with stomatal lines on both surfaces.
Small pollen cones occur in clusters; this conifer has no petals or true flowers.
Ovoid seed cones are approximately erect; their elongated, three-lobed bracts protrude beyond the woody scales.
Azobé

Azobé; red ironwood; ekki

A very large West and Central African rainforest tree, known for exceptionally dense timber. Its leathery simple leaves have pinnate venation, and small flowers are borne in terminal panicles. Native from West Tropical Africa east to Uganda, mainly in humid forests; assessed as Vulnerable by IUCN.
Large evergreen rainforest tree with a tall straight trunk and broad crown.
Alternate, simple, leathery oblong leaves have entire margins and a conspicuous midrib with pinnate lateral veins.
Small white, scented flowers with five petals and numerous stamens occur in terminal panicles.

Nerine sarniensis
Guernsey lily; blood lily

A bulbous South African geophyte with a distinctive seasonal cycle: scarlet flowers emerge on a leafless scape in autumn, while strap-shaped leaves develop later. The strongly recurved tepals and projecting stamens make the flower recognizable. “Guernsey lily” is a common name, not its native range.
Native to the winter-rainfall region of the Western Cape, South Africa; naturalised in a few other places.
Bulbous perennial, dormant in summer; the autumn flowering scape normally appears before the leaves.
Narrow strap-like leaves emerge after flowering and persist through the cooler growing season.
An umbel bears bright red flowers with six narrow, strongly recurved tepals and long stamens.
A three-lobed capsule follows flowering and releases dark seeds.

Opuntia stricta

A spreading coastal prickly pear native to the southeastern United States and nearby Mexico. Its flattened green pads are modified stems, not leaves; areoles bear glochids and sometimes longer spines. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy red-purple fruits. Opuntia species hybridise and vary, so pad shape alone is not a secure field identification.
Native from the southeastern United States through eastern and southern Mexico; widely introduced and invasive in some regions.
Low to spreading succulent shrub composed of flattened cladodes, often forming dense colonies.
True leaves are minute and short-lived; the persistent flat pads are stem segments with areoles and glochids.
Large yellow flowers arise singly from the margins or upper portions of mature pads.

Passiflora incarnata
Purple passionflower; maypop

A perennial North American climbing subshrub with tendrils and deeply three-lobed leaves. Its large flower has white to pale-lavender sepals and petals, a striking purple-and-white filamentous corona and a central reproductive column. The yellow-green berry is often called a maypop; cultivated passion fruit is usually P. edulis, a different species.
Native to the central and eastern United States and Bermuda; introduced and naturalised elsewhere.
Climbing perennial with herbaceous shoots, tendrils and rhizomes that can spread underground.
Alternate leaves are deeply three-lobed with toothed edges; axillary tendrils aid climbing.
Large solitary flowers have five sepals, five petals, several concentric corona rows, five stamens and three styles.
An oval yellow-green berry contains many dark seeds, each surrounded by a pulpy aril.
